work.author: Gregory of Nyssa
work.title: In sanctum Stephanum protomartyrem II
work.edition: Machine translation (claude-opus-5-5, Patristica, 2026-11-01) of: Patrologiae Cursus Completus, Series Graeca, ed. J.-P. Migne (Paris, 1857–1866), vol. 46, cols. 721–734; OCR of scan nnc1.0046978380_ocr (Open Greek and Latin, OGL-PatrologiaGraecaDev)

paragraphs.text: Christ came to dwell in the world for its salvation, and after him the [?] of the Church sprang up. The Witness of the truth shone forth, and the witnesses of the great dispensation shone along with him. The disciples followed the Teacher, walking in the Lord's footsteps: after Christ came the Christ-bearers; after the Sun of righteousness, the lights of the world. And Stephen was the first to blossom for us. He was not woven from Jewish thorns. He was offered to the Lord as the first fruit of the Church's abundance. The Jews wove a crown of thorns and set it on the Savior's head, and so showed the Master of the vineyard fruits worthy of their wicked husbandry, as he had proclaimed beforehand through prophecy, saying: "The vineyard of the Lord of Hosts is the house of Israel, and the man of Judah a beloved new planting. I waited for it to yield grapes, but it yielded thorns." But the workers of the gospel truth offer to the Master, as the first prelude of piety and the first fruits of their husbandry, Stephen, the holy man. He was truly a crown (stephanos), fitted together from many different virtues. First of all, this wonderful man was entrusted with the care of the widows, being attested [?] Another encomium on the holy [?]

by the judgment and choice of the apostles to be a faithful man, full of the Holy Spirit, and also full of the power of spiritual wisdom. By the divine word he showed such advocacy for the preaching that great wonders of divine working accompanied his teachings. "For Stephen," it says, "full of faith and power, did great signs." He did not think it right that his zeal for the widows should hinder him in any way. He held eagerly to the one task and did not neglect the other. This was a great marvel in him, and the mark of an industrious mind. He was entrusted with widows, and he traded for souls. He fed the widows with bread and taught souls with the word. For the one he set a bodily table, and for the other he laid out a spiritual feast. For he was a good man and full of the Holy Spirit. Out of goodness of heart he took on the service of the poor, and by the boldness and power of the Spirit he silenced the enemies of the truth. [?] He resisted, and with the word of truth he overcame them all, "demolishing arguments and every height raised up against the knowledge of God." Such power of speech was in him that, as holy Scripture testifies, no one could withstand the wisdom and the Spirit with which he spoke. But the herald of the truth was led before the council of unbelief.

We must hurry on in this way to pay the Protomartyr what we owe him. Bodily weakness did not allow us to pay it yesterday, and today we must also pay the holy apostles their own commemoration. In the first place, the praises of the saints are not confined to particular days or times: "For the righteous," it says, "will be held in everlasting remembrance." In the second place, those whose minds are not divided are not divided [?]. So there are no martyrs without apostles, and again no apostles apart from martyrs. The apostles are the teachers of the martyrs, and the martyrs are images of the apostles. Blessed Stephen, then, bore their image and stamp [?] cross [?], and through death he was the first to bind on the crown of martyrdom. Yet by enduring martyrdom he brought honor to his teachers and truly became a crown. For the crown of good teachers was not the honor of acclaim but the progress of the Church. As the divine Apostle says, writing to the Corinthians: "My brothers, beloved and longed for, my joy and crown, stand firm in this way."

But let us return to our subject. The Christ-bearer entered the council of the Christ-killers. Into the assembly of wolves leaped

the sheep. It was not simply a sheep caught by beasts, though. It was a sheep shepherded by Christ and contending against the wolves. They [?] and were cut to the quick, biting the flock with accusations and threats. He, however, tore them apart with his refutations more than they tore at him with their threats and accusations. Let us not pass over what is said here barely or superficially. Before such an assembly of evildoers and such an onslaught of wolves, this man dared to speak out boldly against injustice. After that long teaching he said: "Stiff-necked people, uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit, as your fathers did," and the rest. So he appeared on earth, yet beheld as in a mirror the things in heaven. He was clothed in human nature, yet transformed into the face and form of an angel. None of this is unlikely. It was truly fitting for the dignity of the martyrs to be shown in the Protomartyr, so that from then on everyone would know the works of the new grace. The longing for martyrdom not only grants angelic rank but also opens the gates of heaven. It no longer sends souls off to death but commits the spirit into the hands of Christ. The Savior's dominical humanity cried out to his own Father on the cross, saying: "Father, into your hands I commit my spirit." But Stephen, the servant of Christ, reaching up to the Master, says: "Lord Jesus, receive my spirit," and with these words he laid down his soul. The angels received their fellow-dancer, and their praises from above pelted him more than the stones of the Jews from below.

So Stephen, having fought the good fight, received his inheritance in heaven. And all at once the precious stones were woven together into this Stephen, this crown: the most divine heralds of the Gospels, after them the martyrs, and after them again those who shone with saving virtue. First among them are those we commemorate today, flashing out a great and brilliant beauty of piety. I mean Peter, James, and John, the leaders of the apostolic harmony and the crowns of the Church's glory. I do not leave off the name of Stephen. Though I say it many times, countless times, I still thirst and repeat it, for those who await the blessed end of crowns can never have their fill of a crown. So, to speak truthfully, from Stephen we go on to feast again on crowns, and we share in their commemorations, since we hope to share with them, and to remain, and to be glorified with them [?]. For since the promise confirms it,

[?] the fellowship of faith is multiplied. Once more, brothers, we enjoy good things, for the Lord's day of the resurrection shines together with the commemoration of the martyrs. On this day above all, "the illumination of the glory of the gospel of Christ" shone upon our minds. It blossomed in the saving rays of righteousness, wiped out the darkness of impiety, and made souls bright with the knowledge of the truth. And notice, I ask you, what is marvelous and greatest in this benefit. This visible sun rises at dawn and announces the day with the gleams of its forerunning rays. It covers the whole world under heaven and surrounds it with its radiance, but it also hides and dims all the choirs of stars together, so that it alone is seen circling the vaults of heaven. Our Lord Jesus Christ, however, dawned on us from on high, as the prophecy about him says: "by which the Dayspring from on high has visited us." He did not hide the saints who shone like stars before his coming and became his forerunners. He made them even brighter, and he caused other lights to shine along with himself. For the prophets shone out after his coming even more than [?] before it. For dim [?] earth, and having walked about the world under heaven, I am here. [?] Having passed through the world under heaven and walked about the whole of it, I am here. [?]

"I am the light of this world." Though he is the fountain of goodness and came forth from a good Father, he did not disdain to share his own title with those who serve him. He says to his disciples: "You are the light of the world," and: "Let your works shine before people." By the grace of God we will now set out something greater that we can bring forward to recall what has been said. John the Baptist was called a lamp. He was foretold in the Psalms and testified to by the Lord. Speaking in the person of the Father, the Prophet says of him in his hymnody: "I have prepared a lamp for my Christ," that is, I have prepared a servant and forerunner of the light. And the Lord, confirming the Father's voice, says: "He was the burning lamp." Yet although he was a lamp, the coming of the Lord, who was the Sun of righteousness, did not dim him at all. He shone even more, becoming at once the herald and the theologian of the Savior himself, and his Baptist. John, then, was called a lamp [?] because he lit only one house, the house of Israel. But the apostles of the Savior were proclaimed not lamps, nor stars, but great lights. They shone not in one region or one corner but lit up the whole world under heaven.

Their leaders [?] are Peter, James, and John, who are honored today for their witness on Christ's behalf. They ran in harmony to the end of their lives, but they contended in different kinds of martyrdom. The first was shown to be the front-rank leader and chief of the apostolic choir, and he won a glory fitting his rank, honored by suffering as the Savior suffered. Nailed to a cross, he reproduced the Master's image of the King (I call the cross the royal image). He was not ashamed of the suffering but gloried in the great trophy. For neither to them, nor to us, nor to those after us, nor to anyone else [?] of our Lord Jesus Christ, as Paul also says [?]... For this is how Peter, too, clearly held the venerable [?] in honor... Out of great reverence he asked those crucifying him to hang him head-down, so that he would not be equal in glory to the Savior, who was crucified for all humanity and embraced the world with hands spread wide as on the cross. James had his head cut off, hastening to receive his own Head, Christ. For "the head of man is Christ," according to the Apostle, and he is also the head of the whole Church. Blessed John contended in many different struggles during his life and distinguished himself in every achievement of piety. [?] empty into water this [?]

[?] horn... judged [?], he has been counted among the choir of the martyrs [?]. For among those who judge rightly, martyrdom is judged not by the outcome of the suffering but by the choice of the desire. Such, then, were the deaths of those who through death granted an immortal memory to the Churches as well. It was truly fitting for the commemorations of these men to be celebrated together, not only because their piety was in harmony but also because their rank was equal in honor. These three alone were always in the Lord's company. They had, so to speak, a special place and freedom of speech beyond the rest of the apostles, not because of human friendship but by God's true judgment. So we find that at the greatest of the miracles the Lord took only them along, as the most faithful and truest witnesses of what took place. One such occasion was the vision on the mountain. Only Peter, James, and John were there when the Lord transfigured his own body and changed it into a glorious and more brilliant divinity. He set Moses and Elijah beside himself [?], overshadowed them with the cloud of light, and showed them that great image of the kingdom. Another was the daughter of Jairus, whom he raised after she had died, for there too he had these men as eyewitnesses of the miracle. And further, not to linger over each instance, at the very time of his saving passion he took the same men along and [?] ventured to say to them, as to faithful and most steadfast men: "Now my soul is troubled."

We have said these things not to belittle the other apostles but as testimony to the virtue of those we are commemorating. To speak truthfully, it is also a common praise of all the apostles. Deciding who excels or advances further among the saints belongs not to human assessment but to the judgment and truth of God. We have been found worthy to share in the commemorations of such great men, and so we must give thanks. We cannot give as much as we owe, for that is impossible, but we can give as much as we are able, and that is acceptable. The saints ask these honors of us not to gain anything by being praised, but so that we may share in their blessings. And again, that [?] none of the pious [?] or "burning," "into water," "to have this end of life" or "to receive," "judged" [?] is written, will not pay [?]

and John, but of the whole apostolic harmony together, that we celebrate the memorials. According to the truth of doctrine, they hold the rank of members and make up the form of one body. Clearly, then, when one part is glorified [?], as the Apostle says, "all the members are glorified together." This is especially true of those blessed and most perfect men, in whom everything agrees with the truth. Their way of life was of one mind and their faith of one glory. Just as the advantages of their piety are shared, so too is the praise that truth gives them shared. Who would not rightly rejoice and be filled with the Holy Spirit himself on being found worthy to share in the apostolic choir? That choir led the whole world to the knowledge of the truth. It spread the nets of piety over all the world and everywhere set the snares of truth, so that the apostles might catch all humanity together, made savage by wickedness, and bring it to the One who tames and saves. "Their sound has gone out into all the earth." They are the foundations of the Church, the pillars and bulwarks of the truth. They are the ever-flowing springs of salvation, pouring out a great, rich, and godlike stream of teaching. The prophetic voice also sends us to them, saying: "Draw water with joy from the springs of salvation."

Peter is commemorated, the head of the apostles. The other members of the Church are glorified with him, and the Church of God is made firm. By the gift the Lord gave him, he is the unbreakable and most secure rock on which the Savior built the Church. James and John are commemorated in turn. The Savior called them sons of thunder, and they bring all the rain-bearing clouds along with them, for when thunder breaks, the clouds must gather. By clouds we should understand the words of the apostles and the prophets. Their preaching belongs to different times, yet the laws of their piety are in harmony, for their gifts have sprung from one and the same Spirit.

But why should we dare to attempt the impossible and try to commemorate the apostles' virtue as it deserves? Our eagerness to praise is not aimed at Simon, known for his fishing, but at his firm faith, which supports the whole Church. Nor is our speech about the sons of Zebedee, but about the Boanerges, which means "sons of thunder." How will the faint voice of my speech be heard now, when such a great and mighty thunder is resounding in the ears of those standing here? So, having hastened to pay just this much of our gratitude to the saints, we take refuge in

a safe silence. We know well that there is one way we are found worthy to share in the commemorations of the saints: by imitating and emulating their virtues. We should not carry their lives around in our speech but preserve their way of life in our hearts. What will show us to be their true disciples is not habit without reason but piety with reverence, a life like theirs in glory and a way of living like theirs in zeal. Do you honor the memory of the martyrs? Honor their mind as well, for to share in their memory is to agree with their mind. Did "the illumination of the knowledge of the glory of the gospel of Christ" shine on them alone? Was grace sent out to them alone? The commandments are common to all, and the way of life is common to all. There is one judge of the contests and one prize of truth. May we all be found worthy of it, through the prayers and intercessions of the saints we have commemorated, by the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be glory and power for ever and ever. Amen.
